thread.title: Why Facebook needs a leadership overhaul in 2019

author: Anthony Noto
title: Why Facebook needs a leadership overhaul in 2019

organizations.name: george washington university school of business

text: – Reporter, New York Business Journal Dec 26, 2018, 10:58am PST Facebook Inc. didn't have a great 2018. The company's leadership has been scrutinized for a variety of missteps and gaffes, and according to James Bailey , professor and Hochberg Fellow of Leadership Development at the George Washington University School of Business, enough is enough. "It’s time for them to go," Bailey said, referring to CEO and founder Mark Zuckerberg and COO Sheryl Sandberg . Recently, a New York Times investigation showed the Menlo Park, California-based social media giant (NASDAQ: FB) "ran afoul" with its data. Before that, there was the Cambridge Analytica scandal , a gender bias lawsuit , and a data breach that hurt 30 million accounts . It doesn't end there. Facebook has also been scrutinized for allowing users in Myanmar to spread misinformation across the platform and promote violence — partly because its technology is not compatible with the country’s various language fonts. Since then, Facebook has attempted to stymy the calls to violence by banning some 425 pages , 17 groups and 135 user accounts. On Instagram, which Facebook owns , 15 accounts were banned. I discussed with Bailey the severity of these events, what to expect from 2019, and why a graceful exit for Zuckerberg is best for business. These days, many reports make it seem like the wheels are coming off Facebook. Is it hyperbole? At the moment, everyone is in for a “correction.” Counterintuitively, this will benefit Facebook, as the news cycle will cater to the ADD public. Because of the company's tiny overhead and huge margins, investors — including you and me — won’t panic. We’ll sit tight as shares will be comparatively stable and compliment besieged portfolios. In a different climate, Facebook would be punished by Wall Street. Now, not so much. How bad of a year has it been for Facebook and how bad does it have to get before leadership steps down? Facebook's recent record is shady. But you have to remember that the “information” economy is only 30-some years old. There have been no real labor strife or environmental atrocities to galvanize opposition. Thus, only now are data-heavy information technology companies coming under scrutiny. And notice that the public outcry at breeches has been rather soft. Most users know their search patterns are being sold, and (they have) detected no real impact of international hacking. Steal my credit card number or hijack my identity, I’m mightily pissed. Throw questionable political propaganda my way, well, that’s not so different than watching TV news. Zuckerberg and Sandberg have both been scrutinized, the latter most recently in a scathing Vanity Fair article . What needs to change? Is it a matter of resigning or is a cultural overhaul in order? Yeah, it’s time for them to go. We forget that Facebook is not yet 15 years old, which, if we were to draw a human development analogy, makes it an adolescent. My read is that Mark Zuckerberg is also, business maturity-wise, an adolescent. He founded and ushered Facebook, but his skills are no longer well-suited to it surviving and thriving. A graceful exit with a careful succession plan is best. Then Zuckerberg can be serial entrepreneur or global philanthropist. Maybe he’ll buy the Washington Redskins and change their name. Sandberg — hired on a whim — seems tone-deaf and more interested in board positions than being a COO. She’s a talented liability. Cash in an move on. You’ve designed executive programs for companies like Nestle, UBS, ConocoPhillips, and Goldman Sachs. What would you design for Facebook? How would you advise Zuckerberg in responding to the mounting pressure he faces? Assuming the CEO and COO have moved on, the first thing Facebook needs to do is revamp its board. Easier said than done, as boards hold their own power. Still, a diverse, business-tempered board with with a healthy mix of product and service based executives is called for. Facebook is not the only social media source anymore. It’s a commodity, just like Apple (NASDAQ: AAPL) has become. As for executive programming, I’d start at the first layer; the top 200 or so officers, as that’s where everyone else gets their cue from. The first element would be straightforward leadership. These folks have been following for too long. The second would be moving from a cultish to a communal culture. Time for a tonality that the founder didn’t set. Third, accountability, accountability, accountability. Risk management should ascend. Was 2018 a wakeup call or a prelude to tougher days ahead? Commenting on the current political turmoil and its economic repercussions is above my pay grade. But I will say that today’s tumult is tooled for tech transformation. 2018 has been the year of the vanishing CEO — Travis Kalanick (Uber) and Elon Musk (Tesla) being the most poignant examples. Facebook can manage the transition as long as the egos involved are tempered and that it is measured and fairly quick. – Reporter, New York Business Journal Dec 26, 2018, 10:58am PST Wednesday, January 9, 2019 Book of Lists Celebration The Bash is Back!
